strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and well-motivated limitation of existing trajectory-conditioned video generation methods (feature entanglement of robot arm and manipulated object in overlapping regions) and proposes a clear, coherent solution: decomposing the interaction into pre-/interaction/post-interaction phases with a single collaborative trajectory and phase-dependent dominant-subject features.

The experimental protocol is relatively careful: all baselines (Tora, MotionCtrl, DragAnything, IRASim) are retrained on the same dataset with the same backbone (CogVideoX-5B), enabling a fair comparison, and the paper reports both trajectory accuracy, standard video quality metrics (FVD/PSNR/SSIM), VBench dimensions, and a user study.

Ablations (causal embedding, point vs. mask representation, separate vs. collaborative trajectories, cross-attention injection, mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation) directly support each design choice, and the mask-sparsity and perturbation robustness analyses are practically relevant for real user annotation.

Qualitative and in-the-wild results (OOD objects, diverse skills, auto-regressive long video generation) and a user-friendly Gradio annotation interface demonstrate the framework functions as an interactive simulator beyond the benchmark.

The supplementary material provides a detailed automatic data annotation pipeline (CoTracker3 + Grounded-SAM + motion-threshold phase decoupling) yielding ~21k annotated samples, supporting reproducibility and clarity of the training setup.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core idea reduces to re-parameterizing existing multi-trajectory conditioning (as in Tora/DragAnything) into a temporally decomposed single trajectory with object-feature swaps. The architectural components (zero-init conv injection, mask-pooled VAE latents, circular volume) are straightforward combinations of known techniques; no fundamentally new technical machinery is introduced.

Quantitative improvements over the strongest baseline (Tora) are modest (FVD 152.28→147.31, PSNR 21.24→21.55, SSIM 0.788→0.803, TrajError 18.14/26.43→16.47/24.16), and no statistical significance or variance estimates are reported over the 214 test samples, so the claimed SOTA margins could be fragile.

Evaluation is confined to a single dataset (Bridge V2, one robot embodiment, tabletop scenes). The central motivating claim of 'feature entanglement' is supported mainly by qualitative cherry-picked comparisons (Fig 2, Fig 5) rather than a quantitative analysis of overlapping-region quality.

Despite motivating the work by robot data scarcity, the paper never evaluates downstream utility: there is no policy-learning, action extraction, or sim-to-real experiment showing the generated videos actually benefit robot learning, which limits the significance of the claimed 'world simulator' contribution.

The user-defined interaction phase boundaries (F1, F2) and trajectory annotations raise a concern: the TrajError metric compares generated trajectories to input (GT-derived) trajectories, and PSNR/SSIM comparisons use GT trajectories extracted from ground-truth videos, so evaluation conditions may favor methods that faithfully replay GT motion; details of the user study (number of raters, protocol) are also missing.

Only 2D pixel-space trajectories are modeled; the paper acknowledges limited generalization to other embodiments and out-of-domain objects, and the method name 'RoboMaster' collides with the well-known DJI robotics platform, which could cause confusion in the literature.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and clearly motivated problem: trajectory-conditioned video generation that models robot-object interaction rather than isolated object motion, and the 'feature entanglement in overlapping regions' failure mode is convincingly illustrated.

The proposed collaborative trajectory formulation (decomposing the interaction into pre-/interaction/post phases with phase-dependent dominant-object conditioning) is intuitive, well-motivated by the physical dynamics of manipulation, and described in enough detail (Eqs. 3-7, supplementary architecture table) to be reproducible.

Baselines (IRASim, MotionCtrl, DragAnything, Tora) are retrained on the same data and backbone (CogVideoX-5B), making the comparison in Tables 2-3 reasonably fair rather than comparing against numbers from different setups.

Ablations in Table 4 are targeted at each design choice (causal embedding, mask vs. point representation, separate vs. collaborative trajectories, injection mechanism), and additional robustness studies on mask sparsity and trajectory perturbation (Tables 5-6) address practical user-input concerns.

The automatic dataset annotation pipeline (CoTracker3 + Grounded-SAM + motion-threshold phase decoupling) is described and yields ~21k annotated samples; the Gradio annotation demo and long-video auto-regressive generation are useful practical contributions.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is largely a combination of known components (Tora-style plug-and-play motion injection, DragAnything-style mask/entity embeddings, CogVideoX-5B backbone) with the central new idea being a three-phase temporal decomposition of a single trajectory. The 'collaborative' factorization in Eq. 5 is essentially a heuristic conditioning schedule, not a formally derived or principled probabilistic decomposition - the phase boundaries are hard-coded at training/annotation time, and the model's ability to handle ambiguous or user-mis-specified phase boundaries is not analyzed.

The central claim that this generates useful 'robotic decision-making data' is never validated: there is no downstream policy learning or closed-loop evaluation, even though data scarcity for robot learning is the stated motivation. The paper is thus an animation/visual-quality study, and the world-simulator framing is over-claimed relative to the evidence.

Evaluation weaknesses: the test set is small (214 samples from a single dataset, Bridge V2); VBench gains in Table 3 are marginal (often <0.5 points) and within what could be noise; the user study protocol (number of raters, blinding, samples per method) is not described at all, and a 47.33% vs. 20.61% preference gap is hard to interpret without details. In-the-wild generalization (Fig. 6, Fig. S10) is purely qualitative and clearly cherry-picked single successes ('pick up the bee').

The mask-based conditioning may structurally favor the proposed method over point-based baselines (Tora, MotionCtrl) in the mask-heavy metrics; a mask-conditioned variant of the point baseline or an analysis isolating representation vs. trajectory design is only partially provided via the 'w/ Points Representation' ablation, and the fairness of TrajError computation across different input formats is unclear.

Presentation and rigor issues: several equations are sloppy (Eq. 3 mixes variable names x,y vs. i,j and reuses 'i' as both feature index and spatial index; the 'otherwise' case redefines z~d,s[c,x,y] inconsistently); reference [17] and [18] are duplicates; 'Quantative' typos; the causal VAE-latent propagation mechanism is described loosely and its interaction with the phase decomposition (e.g., what happens when the object moves before the annotated F1) is unexamined. Failure-case analysis for the main method is absent except for a brief out-of-domain note in limitations.
No code, model weights, or annotated data release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a system paper whose value depends on the curated 21k-sample pipeline.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: decomposing the interaction process (pre-interaction, interaction, post-interaction) rather than decomposing objects is an intuitive reframing that addresses a real limitation of existing trajectory-controlled video generation methods (feature entanglement in overlapping regions), and this is convincingly illustrated in Fig. 2 and Table 1.

Fair and reasonably comprehensive experimental design: all baselines (Tora, MotionCtrl, DragAnything, IRASim) are retrained on the same curated Bridge V2 data on the same backbone (CogVideoX-5B), which avoids a common unfair-comparison pitfall; the paper evaluates both trajectory accuracy (TrajError) and video quality (FVD, PSNR, SSIM, VBench), plus a user study.

Consistent quantitative gains across metrics (e.g., TrajError_obj 24.16 vs 26.43 for the best baseline; FVD 147.31 vs 152.28) and convincing qualitative comparisons with per-example failure annotations for baselines.

Thorough ablation studies that isolate each design choice (causal embedding, mask vs. point representation, separate vs. collaborative trajectories, injection mechanism), plus robustness analyses (mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation) that directly support the claimed usability benefits.

Good user-facing system design: brush-based mask annotation, phase-based trajectory input, Gradio demo, auto-regressive long-video extension, and a documented automatic dataset annotation pipeline (21k samples) that improves reproducibility.
Honest limitations section covering out-of-domain distortions, 2D-only control, and embodiment generalization.
weaknesses: Incremental technical novelty: the core contribution is a heuristic phase decomposition (dominant/submissive subject) plus a circular-volume embedding and a simple convolutional motion injector; each component is a fairly straightforward modification of existing trajectory-conditioning ideas (Tora, DragAnything), and the factorization in Eq. (5) is informal rather than a principled probabilistic decomposition.

No downstream utility validation: the paper motivates the work by robot data scarcity and frames the model as an 'interactive simulator for producing high-quality robotic data,' but never evaluates whether generated videos actually help policy learning or action inference (e.g., via a learned inverse dynamics model), leaving the central practical claim unsupported.

Evaluation scale is modest: 214 test samples from a single dataset (Bridge V2) with a fixed robot embodiment; in-the-wild generalization is shown only qualitatively (Figs. 6, S10, S11) without quantitative metrics or human evaluation, and details of the user study (number of raters, protocol, variance) are missing.

Several technical details are unclear or inconsistent: Eq. (3) has apparent index/format errors (x, y vs. i, j; z-tilde 'otherwise' branch), the radius r ∝ mask area relationship is given only proportionally without the constant, the interaction-phase boundary detection threshold τ is not specified, and Equations (5)-(7) conflate latent-space and pixel-space notations.

VBench improvements are marginal (often <1 point on several axes) and within a range that could reflect noise; no error bars or statistical significance are reported for any quantitative comparison, including the user study preference split (47.33%).

Some writing issues: duplicated reference entries ([17]/[18] are identical), minor typos ('Quantative', 'Deviration'), and the ablation 'w/ Cross Attention' baseline is described too briefly to understand how the alternative was implemented.
No statement about code or model release, which limits reproducibility for a system-heavy paper.

strengths: The collaborative trajectory formulation—decomposing the interaction process into pre-/interaction/post-interaction phases and modeling each phase with the dominant object—is a sensible and clearly motivated solution to the feature-entanglement problem in multi-object trajectory control, and is well differentiated from prior work (Tora, DragAnything, IRASim) as summarized in Table 1.

Evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area: quantitative metrics (FVD, PSNR, SSIM, TrajError), a user study, VBench metrics, qualitative comparisons, and—importantly—a downstream robotic action-planning pipeline on both RLBench and SIMPLER that directly tests the practical value of generated videos for policy learning.

Baselines (Tora, MotionCtrl, DragAnything, IRASim, TesserAct, OpenVLA) are retrained/fine-tuned on the same curated dataset and backbone for fairness, which strengthens the credibility of the SOTA claims.

The ablation study is thorough and well designed: causal embedding, point- vs mask-based representation, separate vs collaborative trajectories, cross-attention injection, plus robustness analyses on mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation, and imperfect prompts—all ablated on the full benchmark.

The paper contributes a 21k annotated video–trajectory dataset with a documented semi-automatic annotation pipeline (CoTracker3 + Grounded-SAM + human-in-the-loop), and the appendix honestly discusses annotation failure rates and remaining limitations (OOD objects, robot morphology generalization, 2D-only control).
weaknesses: Core novelty is moderate: the technical ingredients (trajectory latent injection via zero-init conv layers, mask-based object embeddings, plug-and-play injectors) largely follow the existing Tora/ControlNet-style recipe; the main contribution is the phase-decomposition heuristic rather than a fundamentally new modeling principle. The three-phase switching (vd → vs → vd) is an engineering design choice supported empirically but not analyzed theoretically.

Improvement margins over the strongest baseline (Tora) are modest on some metrics (e.g., FVD 147.31 vs 152.28, SSIM 0.803 vs 0.788), and the downstream action-planning results (Table 4) are mixed—RoboMaster loses to Tora on 'put knife' and 'open microwave' and is second-best on several others, which somewhat weakens the claim of uniformly more reliable interaction videos.

The user study (45.16% preference) lacks essential details: number of participants, evaluation protocol, statistical significance testing, and what aspects were judged; as presented it is hard to interpret.

The method requires users to specify interaction phase boundaries (F1, F2) and separate sub-trajectories, which partially offsets the claimed annotation simplicity; the user-interaction benefit is asserted more than measured.

The evaluation protocol has ambiguities: TrajError computation for generated videos (presumably via tracking) is not fully specified; PSNR/SSIM against GT are known to be unreliable for generative models; and the test set (214 samples) is small, with no variance or significance reporting.

The framework is trained/fine-tuned on a strong 5B backbone with fixed camera and per-benchmark post-training, so the extent to which gains come from the proposed trajectory design vs. the pretrained prior is not fully disentangled.
Multiple typos and writing issues (e.g., 'establishs', 'Quantative', 'Comparision', 'or the second stage', 'Deviration', 'Frechét') suggest insufficient proofreading.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: trajectory-controlled video generation as a data source for robotic manipulation, with a focus on multi-object interaction that prior works (Tora, DragAnything, IRASim) do not explicitly handle.

The proposed decomposition of the interaction process into pre-interaction / interaction / post-interaction phases, with phase-dependent conditioning on the dominant subject, is a simple but sensible design, and is well-motivated by the observed feature-entanglement failure mode.

The experimental scope is relatively broad: quantitative comparisons (FVD, PSNR, SSIM, trajectory error), a user study, VBench metrics, robustness ablations (mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation, imperfect prompts), and — notably — a downstream evaluation where generated videos are converted to actions via an inverse dynamics model and executed on RLBench and SIMPLER, which connects video quality to actual robot performance.

All trajectory baselines are retrained on the same curated 21k Bridge dataset with the same backbone (CogVideoX-5B), which makes the main comparison (Tab. 2) more fair than simply citing numbers from prior papers.

Comprehensive ablations support the main design choices (causal embedding, mask vs. point representation, collaborative vs. separate trajectories, injection mechanism), and the appendix documents the dataset construction pipeline and architecture in reasonable detail.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core contributions are largely engineering refinements over existing trajectory-conditioned video generation: the 'collaborative trajectory' is a heuristic phase-based switching between robot-arm and object trajectories, and the mask-based appearance/shape embedding is close in spirit to DragAnything. The framework is a straightforward combination of known components rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea.

Several technical inconsistencies and sloppiness undermine confidence: (1) the claim of outperforming Tora on '8 out of 10 tasks' does not match Table 4, which contains 9 tasks where RoboMaster wins 7; (2) Eq. 3 has index errors (i used as both channel and spatial index, undefined x,y); (3) Eq. 5 is presented as a probabilistic factorization but is really a heuristic conditioning scheme, since the conditioned variables are not properly marginalized; (4) the circular volume radius r is defined only up to an unspecified proportionality constant.

Evaluation weaknesses: the main benchmark uses only 214 test samples, which makes FVD and PSNR estimates noisy, with no variance or significance reporting; the user study methodology (number of participants, protocol, how Preference is normalized) is entirely unspecified; TrajError units are not defined; PSNR/SSIM against a single GT video is a questionable metric for stochastic generative models.

The three-phase decomposition assumes a rigid manipulation structure (robot arm leads before/after, object is 'submissive' during interaction) and requires transition timestamps F1, F2 — either annotated automatically with a motion threshold that may fail on complex contact-rich skills, or supplied by the user at inference, which weakens the claimed user-friendliness.

All results are in 2D pixel space with fixed cameras and limited robot morphologies; the downstream action-planning evaluation post-trains on only 1,300 clips and the success-rate gains over Tora are modest and mixed on several tasks (e.g., put knife 0.76 vs 0.82, open microwave 0.54 vs 0.61), so the central claim that better interaction modeling yields better policies is only weakly supported.

Writing quality is below par for a top venue: multiple typos and grammatical errors ('establishs', 'Quantative', 'or the second stage' missing a letter, 'shows promise'), undefined symbols at first use, and an abstract claiming 'new state-of-the-art' with margins that are small on several metrics (e.g., FVD 147.31 vs 152.28).

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and well-motivated problem: existing trajectory-controlled video generation methods treat robot-arm and object trajectories as independent, causing feature entanglement during interaction. The proposed phase-decomposed 'collaborative trajectory' is a sensible, clearly articulated solution.

Evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area: Bridge video-quality/trajectory metrics with retrained baselines on the same backbone (fair comparison), VBench metrics, a user study, ablations of each component (causal embedding, mask vs. point representation, separate vs. collaborative trajectories, injection mechanism), plus a downstream robotic action-planning evaluation on RLBench and SIMPLER with success rates over 100 trials per task.

The paper contributes a curated 21k video–trajectory dataset from Bridge with a documented automatic annotation pipeline (CoTracker3 + Grounded SAM + human-in-the-loop filtering), which has independent value for the community.
Robustness analyses (mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation, imperfect prompts) address practical usability concerns and are often missing from similar papers.
The appendix honestly discusses limitations, including Grounded-SAM annotation failure rates (0.14/0.67) and generalization limits to novel robot morphologies, which strengthens credibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than groundbreaking. The overall recipe (pre-trained DiT backbone + plug-and-play convolutional trajectory injection + mask-based object embedding) closely follows Tora/DragAnything; the core contribution is the temporal phase decomposition and switching of the conditioning latent (vd → vs → vd), which is a relatively simple design change. The claimed factorization in Eq. (5) is conceptually straightforward rather than a deep technical innovation.

Some technical presentation is imprecise or contains errors: Eq. (3) has inconsistent index notation (mixing i, x, y and reusing i as channel and spatial indices), the radius heuristic r ∝ mask area is heuristic and unstated in scale, and the paper never explains why a circular (disc-shaped) latent volume is appropriate for non-circular objects like a spoon or cloth.

The evaluation set is small (214 Bridge test samples), no confidence intervals or variance are reported anywhere, and several quantitative margins are modest (e.g., FVD 147.31 vs. 152.28; SSIM 0.803 vs. 0.788), so the SOTA claim rests on small gaps. The user-study methodology (number of raters, setup, what 'Preference %' means when values do not obviously aggregate) is under-specified.

In the downstream action-planning results (Table 4), RoboMaster actually loses to Tora on two tasks (put knife 0.76 vs 0.82; open microwave 0.54 vs 0.61), which weakens the 'more reliable interaction videos' narrative; this is mentioned but not analyzed.

The method still requires users to specify temporal boundaries of the interaction phase (start/end timestamps) — precisely the annotation burden the introduction criticizes in prior work; the mitigation via automatic decoupling is only for training data, not user inference.

No explicit statement of code or dataset release, limiting reproducibility of a system-level contribution; writing also contains a number of typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 'Quantative', 'Deviration', 'Frechét', 'establishs', 'or the second stage') that should have been cleaned up.
The qualitative comparison figures (Figs. 2, 5, 7) appear selectively chosen; failure cases of the proposed method on the Bridge benchmark are not shown, only out-of-domain limitations.
